Sumimi v0.5.0 — **the identity is rebuilt, Umami's own tracker now talks to
Sumimi, and the privacy page stops promising things the code does not do**.

This is a **breaking release**: the event table is a new shape (schema v10), the
raw address and the raw user agent are **not stored by default any more**, and
an existing instance is **not migrated** — the old database is set aside.

---

## One: three identifiers, sixteen bytes each, and the session start as a fact

The event row now carries three identifiers, and each one says what it is:

| column | what it is | who gives it | how it is made |
|---|---|---|---|
| `visitor_id` | **the visitor** | the server | `SHA-256(address ‖ user_agent ‖ website_id)` |
| `visit_id` | **one stretch of activity** (a session) | the server | `SHA-256(visitor_id ‖ the second it started)` |
| `user_id` | **the visitor as the site owner knows them** | the client | the client's `id`, hashed |

**Sixteen bytes each** — the same width as Umami's, and the same width as the
shape this project had before v8. The eight-byte variant is **deferred, not
cancelled**: it is measurably smaller, but one shape for both identifiers is
worth more than the last 20% of the disk, and the upgrade path that would carry
it is not ready (see the last section).

**The session start is stored, not derived.** A `session_start` column holds the
moment the stretch began. It is a fact about what happened, so it is written
down rather than worked out of a bucket — and it is the anchor for the
duration report.

**The visitor identifier is a hash of the address and the user agent**, and the
address that goes in is **the whole IPv4 address, or the /64 of an IPv6 one**.
Not a /24: a /24 is 256 addresses, so everyone behind one office NAT or one
campus network counted as one visitor. IPv6 keeps its /64 because the privacy
extensions rotate everything after it.

**The raw address and the raw user agent are not stored by default.** What is
kept is the hash — the visitor identifier — and the readings: country, region,
city, browser, system, device. `SUMIMI_STORE_RAW=1` keeps the raw strings as
well; that is the site owner's choice, not ours. (Umami does not store them
either, so the defaults match, and the numbers are comparable.)

---

## Two: Umami's tracker, unmodified, now talks to Sumimi

The collection flow is now **1:1 with Umami's**, and the proof is a test: Umami's
own tracker, compiled from its source and run in a real browser, points at a
Sumimi server and its events land.

* **The client carries the session.** The server answers
  `{cache, sessionId, visitId}` — Umami's own key names — and the client sends
  the `cache` token back on the next hit. `x-sumimi-cache` is read first, and
  `x-umami-cache` second; the same for the website id and the hostname.
* **The token is signed, not encrypted.** The client can read it; it cannot
  change it.
* **The server keeps no state.** The session's start and its last activity live
  in the token, so a session is cut by a 30-minute idle timeout wherever the
  request lands — no shared cache, nothing to lose on a restart.
* **CORS.** The collection endpoints answer preflights, so a tracker on another
  origin works at all. (They did not: the browser's preflight failed, the
  tracker swallowed the error, and nothing was collected. Cross-origin
  collection was silently dead.)
* **`type: "performance"` and `type: "error"`** are accepted; an error report
  is not stored and does not count as an event.
* **`payload.timestamp`** is honoured, so a client that buffered events can send
  them with the time they happened.

The response's `sessionId` is Sumimi's visitor identifier and `visitId` is its
session — the names are Umami's, the meanings are documented on the
[API page](https://sumimi.dev/api/).

---

## Three: the bots are tagged, not dropped — and the dashboard can ask for them

A crawler is **not dropped**. It is stored and **marked**, and the marked
traffic is **not part of the numbers** — unless the dashboard asks for it.

The markers are a **taxonomy**, not a flag:

| group | kinds |
|---|---|
| `bot-ai` | `bot-ai-openai`, `bot-ai-anthropic`, `bot-ai-perplexity`, `bot-ai-apple` |
| `bot-se` | `bot-se-google`, `bot-se-bing`, `bot-se-yandex`, `bot-se-baidu`, `bot-se-other` |
| `bot-social` | `bot-social-meta`, `bot-social-x`, `bot-social-linkedin`, `bot-social-messaging` |
| `bot-other` | `bot-other-unknown` |
| `dev` | the developer's own traffic (`user_id` is `developer`, `manager` or `owner`) |
| `test` | `user_id` is `tester` |

**AI crawlers are their own group**, because a crawler that reads a page to
answer a question is not the same animal as one that reads it to build an index
— and the first question a site owner asks is "how many AI crawlers came?".
Picking a group picks all its kinds; picking kinds picks them one by one.

**A marker is not a label.** A marker is written by the server. A label is the
site owner's own (`data-tag="campaign"`), and it only groups things — it never
changes a number. The two are kept apart, because a filter that excluded
everything tagged would throw the owner's own campaign traffic out of the
numbers.

---

## Four: the privacy page now says what the code does

The privacy page is written as **acceptance criteria for this project's own
design** — so every sentence in it has to be true. Nine of them were not, and
they are now:

* the address and the user agent were promised to be stored — **they are not**,
  by default, and the switch that turns them on is named;
* "a visitor *is* the pair (prefix, user agent)" became "the visitor identifier
  is `SHA-256(address ‖ user_agent ‖ website_id)`";
* the /24 is now the whole IPv4 address, and the /64 for IPv6;
* the session identifier is sixteen bytes, not eight;
* the query string is kept by default — the page contradicted itself about it;
* **Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are sent by default**, and
  `data-do-not-track="true"` honours them (Umami's way, and the owner's
  decision: *protecting privacy* means not deciding for the site owner);
* **there is no per-request access log at all** — the page described one;
* "the server never makes an outbound request" was wrong twice: the uptime
  checks go to the sites you listed, and `--ssl` talks to the ACME provider.
  What is true is that **nothing that carries your data away ever leaves the
  box** — no telemetry, no crash reporting, no update check;
* the FAQ's claim that the visitor identifier is derived from the server secret
  was wrong — it is not, so **changing the secret invalidates the issued
  tokens but keeps the visitors the same**.

---

## Five: the Chinese assistant's months

「本月」and 「上个月」 asked for the thirty days **before** this month — both of
them, in both languages' sense of the words. The English "this month" asked
for the days from the first until now, so **the two languages disagreed, and
the Chinese one was wrong**. They now answer the same windows.

---

## Also in this release

* **the tracker** sends the page view as soon as the document is ready, carries
  the signed token, and reports the web vitals once per document;
* **the report's cache key** includes the marker selection, so two dashboards
  asking for different traffic do not share an answer;
* **the audience count** is the number of distinct visitor identifiers;
* **the geolocation database** is downloaded by you (`sumimi geoip download`),
  so the server still never reaches out for it;
* **the DuckDB finding**: version 2.0.0 silently drops rows that another
  connection commits while an `ALTER TABLE` is running. **Stop the writers
  before changing a column's type.** The reproduction and the upstream
  evidence are in the issue tracker.

---

## Upgrading

1. Stop the server.
2. Start it once. The old database is **set aside**, not migrated — the events
   and the website registrations in it stay in the file next to the new one
   (`*.v9.bak`), the accounts do not (they live in the instance store).
3. If you want the raw address and the raw user agent back, set
   `SUMIMI_STORE_RAW=1`.

The Umami-compatible API is unchanged, so an existing Umami tracker keeps
working — and now works across origins.
